Seward wrote in a firm tone but had to avoid pushing Britain into the war on the Southern side. His instructions walked that line again and again. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d363:
The American answer to London on 17 January 1863 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 363 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d463:
The letter printed as document 463 was written on 16 April 1863 by Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary William H. Seward. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d563:
Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons directed a letter to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State on 13 June 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the early summer of 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d663:
The 14 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out.
plos-pbio-0020163:
Mazahir T. Hasan, Rainer W. Friedrich, Thomas Euler, and co-workers built a glowing sensor mouse in PLOS Biology in 2004. Their mice make fluorescent proteins that light up when calcium rises inside cells. Calcium spikes are a basic signal in nerve and muscle cells, so the glow reports cell activity.

A drug switch called TET control lets researchers turn the sensor on only when and where they want. That keeps the sensor from disturbing growth when it is not needed. With it, activity in living brain tissue can be watched under a microscope. The tool opened a path to watching whole circuits at work, a goal that later calcium imaging methods built on.
plos-pbio-0020363:
Bino John, Anton J. Enright, Alexei Aravin, and a large team predicted microRNA targets in humans in PLOS Biology in 2004. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that tune gene activity by binding to messenger RNAs. Each one may control hundreds of messages, but finding which ones was a fresh problem at the time.

The team wrote rules for spotting likely binding sites across human messages and tested them against known cases. Their target list gave the young field a map to work from. MicroRNAs are now known to shape development, immunity, and cancer. Early maps like this one set the terms for how targets are predicted and checked, and they remain a base that later methods refined.
plos-pone-0000063:
David G. Haskell, Jonathan P. Evans, and Neil W. Pelkey compared bird life across land uses in PLOS ONE in 2006. They surveyed birds in plantations, in forests, and in exurban areas, the low-density spread at a city's edge. Plantation land held far fewer bird kinds than the other two.

The authors call that bird life depauperate, thinned out. Forests held the richest mix, as expected, but exurban areas did better than plantations despite their houses and roads. The contrast warns that not all human land use is equal for wildlife. Tree plantations managed as single crops can be poorer habitat than lightly settled land. That ranking can guide land choices where birds are a concern.
plos-pone-0000163:
Frédéric Lemaire, Céline A. Mandon, Julien Reboud, and colleagues published this toxicology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It describes toxicity assays run in nanodrops, droplets so small that hundreds of tests fit in a tiny volume. The assays combine a living bioassay with morphometric endpoints, measurements of shape and form in the test organisms.

Small-scale tests use far less of a test chemical and far fewer animals. The authors show that nanodrop assays can still read out meaningful harm. The method points toward cheaper, higher-volume screening of chemicals and drugs, where testing capacity is often the bottleneck.
plos-pone-0000263:
Andreas Lamanda, Zeinab Cheaib, Melek Dilek Turgut, and colleagues published this biochemistry paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Proteins in saliva buffer acids, soaking up protons to protect teeth and the mouth. The authors study protein buffering in simple model systems and in whole human saliva, comparing the two.

Understanding saliva's buffering explains part of how the mouth resists acid attacks after eating. The authors measure how much of that protection comes from proteins rather than other components. The results have practical bearing on dental research and on designing artificial saliva for patients who make too little.
plos-pone-0000363:
Oren Kobiler, Assaf Rokney, and Amos B. Oppenheim wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study about lambda, a virus that infects bacteria. After entering a host cell, the virus faces a choice: multiply fast and burst the cell open, or stay quiet inside the host's DNA. Their work centers on one viral protein, CIII, that helps steer that choice.

CIII works by blocking a protease, an enzyme that cuts other proteins apart. By slowing that enzyme down, CIII helps tip the virus toward the quiet, dormant path. Working out how one small protein guides this switch helps explain how viruses balance attack and hiding, a basic question in virus biology.
plos-pone-0000463:
Gabriel del Rio and colleagues found a shared sequence pattern in a family of cell-death-related receptors, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dependence receptors are proteins that can trigger a cell to die when their partner molecule is absent. The team identified a novel motif, a recurring pattern of amino acids, in these receptors.

A shared motif is a clue to shared machinery: it marks the part of the receptor that likely does the common work. Motifs give biologists a handle for finding new family members in genome data and for guessing how the death signal is sent. Dependence receptors matter in development and in cancer, where their fail-safe killing can be lost.
plos-pone-0000563:
Eric Waltari and colleagues compared two ways of finding where species survived the ice ages, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Pleistocene refugia are the sheltered pockets where species waited out glacial cold. The team compared phylogeographic predictions, from DNA evidence, with ecological niche model predictions, from climate and habitat data, for locating those refugia.

Where the two methods agree, confidence is high; where they differ, each exposes the other's blind spots. Refugia matter now because they are often today's biodiversity hotspots and tomorrow's climate shelters. The study is a methods check with direct conservation use.
plos-pone-0000663:
Jack Merrin, Stanislas Leibler and John S. Chuang turned an inkjet printer into a tool for placing living bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many studies of interacting microbes need cells deposited in precisely defined patterns. Ordinary methods make that slow or costly. Their printer is piezoelectric, adapted from a design first built to print DNA microarrays.

The authors describe the device as inexpensive, and it can print patterns using multiple bacterial strains. Printing living cells like ink lets researchers set up microbial neighborhoods on purpose. Ecologists can then watch competition and cooperation unfold from known starting positions, a control that mixed cultures never offer.
plos-pone-0000763:
Michaela Frye, Amanda G. Fisher and Fiona M. Watt characterized skin stem cells by the chemical marks on their DNA packaging. Switching on the gene Myc pushes epidermal stem cells to leave their niche. They then turn into sebocytes and surface skin. The shift is tied to wide changes in gene transcription. Marks on histones, the packaging proteins, help set which genes can be read.

The team identified chromatin modifications characteristic of epidermal stem cells across the whole genome. Their title says these global marks define the stem cells, and that Myc-driven differentiation alters them. A signature of marks could let researchers recognize true stem cells without waiting for behavior.
plos-pone-0000863:
Murali Gururajan, Joshy Jacob and Bali Pulendran studied toll-like receptors in mouse B cells for PLOS ONE in 2007. Toll-like receptors are sensors that spot patterns found on germs and switch on the body's first line of defense. The team compared B cells from the spleen with B cells from mucosal tissue, the moist linings that meet the outside world.

For each cell group they asked which receptors are present and how strongly the cells respond when those receptors are triggered. The work maps immune sensing across two very different settings. It helps explain how B cells help start a broader immune response after they meet a threat.
plos-pone-0000963:
Ryan Nitta, Catherine Smith and Brian Kennedy tested how the retinoblastoma protein is broken down in cells missing certain lamins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lamins A and C are filaments that brace the cell nucleus. They are also needed to keep the retinoblastoma protein, a brake on cell growth, stable, though the route was unknown.

Two cancer linked proteins, gankyrin and MDM2, were natural suspects for the breakdown. The team report the loss runs through the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, but independently of both suspects. Ruling out the obvious routes is real progress. It tells the field where the true mechanism is not.
plos-pone-0001063:
Walter Weiss, Anita Kumar, George Jiang and colleagues tested a combined malaria vaccine in rhesus monkeys, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their earlier design used four antigens: DNA plasmids first, then a poxvirus boost. It protected a high percentage of monkeys against Plasmodium knowlesi malaria.

The vaccine covers several life stages of the parasite, including two blood stage antigens. This study asks how much protection depends on optimal DNA priming and on including those blood stage parts. Taking a working vaccine apart, piece by piece, shows which parts carry the protection. That knowledge is what lets a monkey success become a human candidate.
plos-pone-0001163:
Mucins are the main ingredients of mucus, and their genes contain long repetitive stretches that are hard to read. Yun Hee Jeong and colleagues examined one such gene, MUC2, in relation to stomach cancer, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The repetitive region, called a minisatellite, varies between people.

The authors report that rare versions of this repeat region influence susceptibility to gastric carcinoma. Mucin genes are well studied for how much protein they make, but their genomic variation is murkier because the repeats resist standard analysis. The study shows that even awkward repetitive DNA can carry disease risk.
plos-pone-0001263:
Keeping time, judging how long things last, depends on a network that includes the basal ganglia. Christian Beste and colleagues studied time processing in Huntington's disease, where the basal ganglia deteriorate, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Timing processes were already known to change in the disease.

This group-control study compared timing performance in Huntington's patients with healthy controls. Because the structures important for timing are also critical for the movement problems of Huntington's, the work links two features of one disease. Results like these can serve as sensitive measures of how the disease progresses.
plos-pone-0001363:
For HIV-positive mothers in low-resource settings, breastfeeding is often the only safe feeding option, yet it can transmit the virus. Louise Kuhn and colleagues followed mothers and infants in Zambia to study exclusive breastfeeding, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Clear data on the benefits of exclusive breastfeeding for HIV prevention were needed to encourage breastfeeding support programs.

The authors report high uptake of exclusive breastfeeding and reduced early post-natal HIV transmission where replacement feeding is unsafe. Mixed feeding had been thought riskier than exclusive breastfeeding; their data support promoting the exclusive pattern. The findings influenced infant feeding guidance for HIV-infected women.
plos-pone-0001463:
Zhiping Wang, Shicui Zhang, and Guangfeng Wang wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how fish eggs fend off germs. Fish that lay eggs in open water leave them amid dense microbes. How the young live through those attacks was not known. The team tested the fluid inside fresh zebrafish eggs.

They show the egg fluid can kill germs on its own. The killing comes from defense parts passed from the mother. That maternal guard covers the days before the young fish can make its own defense. The finding adds a neat chapter to how animals protect their young at the most frail stage.
plos-pone-0001563:
Alassane Dicko and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot for children in Mali. The shot blends proteins from two strains of the blood stage parasite. A past phase 1 trial in adults in Mali had cleared the way. This trial moved the shot into young children, the group at most risk.

The team checked safety and immune replies in the children step by step. A shot that is safe in adults can act unlike in young children. Child data are thus the true gate for a malaria vaccine. This trial is a key rung on that climb.
plos-pone-0001663:
P. K. Vinod, Neelanjan Sengupta, P. J. Bhat, and their co-authors mapped how three signaling pathways jointly control a yeast gene in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, adapts to its surroundings to survive. When nitrogen runs low, it grows in chains of stretched cells called pseudohyphae, which help it forage. The switch is driven by a gene named FLO11.

The study integrates the cAMP-PKA, MAPK, and TOR pathways, three major signal routes that sense food and stress. The full text gives the model, the gene activity data, and how each pathway's push on FLO11 adds up. Yeast is a stand-in for cells in general, so rules found here guide work on how cells combine signals to make one decision.
plos-pone-0001763:
Heather Sadlish, Heike Rampelt, James Shorter, and their co-authors studied helper proteins that manage yeast prions in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Prions are proteins that fold into self-copying shapes. In yeast they create heritable traits. The cytosolic chaperone network, the cell's protein-folding crew, is closely tied to prion emergence and maintenance. The Hsp110 chaperone Sse1 exchanges nucleotides for Hsp70 chaperones.

The team reports that Hsp110 chaperones regulate prion formation and propagation through two discrete activities. The full text gives the yeast experiments and the activity separation. Yeast prions are a safe stand-in for the protein clumping behind human diseases like Alzheimer's, so their control crew is studied worldwide.
plos-pone-0001863:
Uri Yerushalmi and Mina Teicher used computer simulations of evolution to study timing in neural processing in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Recent studies suggested some neural mechanisms rest on the fine timing structure of spiking activity, the exact timing of nerve spikes. Less effort had gone into how such mechanisms evolve: could they arise, and must they?

Running such simulations, the authors argue temporal elements in neural processing are inevitable: selection produces them without being asked. The full text gives the simulation setup and the evolved networks. If timing codes arise inevitably, then brain labs should expect them in all brains, not as rare inventions of certain brains.
plos-pone-0001963:
Akira Kinjo and Haruki Nakamura analyzed what makes a protein family's signature, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Labs spot distant kinship between proteins by comparing them to a position-specific scoring matrix, a table that scores each spot in a sequence. Those tables seem to hold the essence of a family, but what that essence is made of was unclear.

The pair applied singular value analysis, a math tool that splits a table into ranked parts, to many such matrices. Their aim was to see which parts carry the family stamp. Knowing the anatomy of a signature can make homology searches sharper and faster.
plos-pone-0002063:
Isabelle Lombaert and co-authors rescued spit glands with stem cells after radiation, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Head and neck cancer is the fifth most common cancer, and survival is fairly high. Yet radiation often wrecks the salivary glands, leaving patients with dry mouths and a much poorer quality of life.

The team transplanted stem cells into irradiated glands in their model. As the title states, the transplant rescued gland function after the damage. A working rescue in animals is a first step toward giving cancer survivors back a basic comfort that radiation takes away.
plos-pone-0002163:
Crystal Jaing, Shea Gardner, Kevin McLoughlin, and co-authors built a gene chip for spotting the weapons of harmful bacteria, described in PLOS ONE in 2008. Known and unknown germs pose a steady threat to public health, and fast tools to detect and describe them are badly needed. Existing tests cannot cover the full range of what makes a microbe dangerous.

The team's functional gene array carries probes for bacterial virulence elements, the genes that let bacteria cause disease. A single test can scan a sample for many such genes at once. Tools like this help health teams name a threat early, before an outbreak grows legs.
plos-pone-0002263:
Farrel Buchinsky, Joseph Donfack, Craig Derkay, and co-authors studied children and adults with a rare airway disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis grows wart-like tumors in the airway, causing hoarseness and trouble breathing. It is caused by human papillomavirus types 6 or 11, and its course varies hugely, with patients needing repeated surgeries to keep the airway open.

The team compared cases by HPV type and by age at diagnosis. They report that the child's age, more than the virus type, tracks with how the disease behaves. That ordering helps doctors counsel families on what course to expect.
plos-pone-0002363:
Ted Cohen, Caroline Colijn, and Bryson Finklea asked whether surveys understate the burden of drug-resistant tuberculosis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. TB strains resistant to many first- and second-line antibiotics challenge a global strategy built on standard drug regimens. Highly resistant strains had already been blamed in outbreaks. Survey-based estimates guide the money and drugs sent to fight them.

The team used a simulation study to test how those estimates are built. Their modeling suggests survey methods can miss part of the true burden, for instance where resistant cases die or are treated outside the system. Getting the count right decides whether control programs are sized for the epidemic they actually face.
plos-pone-0002463:
Stjernman joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Martin Stjernman, Lars Råberg, Jan-Åke Nilsson, among others. Its subject is maximum Host Survival at Intermediate Parasite Infection Intensities. Although parasitism has been acknowledged as an important selective force in the evolution of host life histories.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002563:
Corcoran led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Kelly E. Corcoran, Katarzyna A. Trzaska, Helen Fernandes, among others. Its subject is mesenchymal Stem Cells in Early Entry of Breast Cancer into Bone Marrow.

BCCs can achieve quiescence, without interfering with hematopoiesis. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002663:
A 2008 study by Rafael Sanjuán and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up a network model for the correlation between epistasis and genomic complexity. Authorship is credited in the record to Rafael Sanjuán and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The study of genetic interactions (epistasis) is central to the understanding of genome organization and evolution. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002763:
Lee Alan Dugatkin and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on cheating on the edge. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Lee Alan Dugatkin, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. We present the results of an individual agent-based model of antibiotic resistance in bacteria. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002863:
Bilada Bilican and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was induction of olig2 + precursors by FGF involves BMP signalling blockade at the smad level. The catalog record names Bilada Bilican first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. During normal development oligodendrocyte precursors (OPCs) are generated in the ventral spinal cord in response to Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signalling. It goes on to note a further point. There is also a second, late wave of oligodendrogenesis in the dorsal spinal cord independent of Shh activity. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002963:
Christopher Love, Shuguang Zhang and Andreas Mershin chased the source of a steady voltage in a potted fig tree in 2008. It has long been known that many plants hold an electrical potential between their xylem, the water-carrying tissue, and the soil. What creates that voltage stayed controversial for years.

After ruling out stray capacitive and inductive effects from the setup, the team probed the sustained difference in a Ficus benjamina tree. Published in PLOS ONE, the quirky study treats a textbook curiosity with care. Its results bear on claims that trees might serve as living power sources.
plos-pone-0003063:
Amit Bharadwaj, Sadhu Leelavathi, Sudeshna Mazumdar-Leighton and co-authors studied a heat- and alkali-tough enzyme in 2008. Understanding protein stability under several extreme conditions at once remains a major challenge. The xylanase from Bacillus sp. NG-27, called BSX, works best at high temperature and alkaline pH and resists denaturants.

A partly exposed valine at the protein's start plays a critical role in stabilizing it, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, one residue with an outsized effect is a neat lesson for enzyme engineering, where industrial users prize exactly this toughness. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003163:
Alma Fulurija, Thomas A. Lutz, Katja Sladko and colleagues test vaccination against the hormone GIP as an obesity treatment in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The World Health Organization counted more than one billion people worldwide as overweight and at risk of chronic illness, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and stroke. Current therapies showed limited efficacy and often had unpleasant side effects.

The authors explore blocking GIP by vaccination as a fresh route to weight control. Readers get a bold idea tested at an early stage. Even readers who doubt the approach will find the reasoning useful for judging obesity research claims.
plos-pone-0003263:
Lauren McDaniel, Mya Breitbart, Jennifer Mobberley and colleagues sequence viruses from Tampa Bay in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Phage integrase genes often play a role in establishing lysogeny in temperate phage, by catalyzing integration of the phage into one of the host's replicons. To investigate temperate phage gene expression, an induced viral metagenome from Tampa Bay was sequenced by 454 methods.

Readers get a metagenomic analysis of lysogeny, the state where a virus hides in its host, and implications for prophage gene expression. Coastal virus communities affect marine bacteria and carbon flow, so their hidden state matters to ocean ecology.
plos-pone-0003363:
Søren Søgaard Lund, Lise Tarnow, Anne Sofie Astrup and colleagues trial metformin in type 1 diabetes in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite intensive insulin treatment, many patients with type 1 diabetes have longstanding inadequate glycaemic control. Metformin is an oral hypoglycaemic agent that improves insulin action in patients with type 2 diabetes. The team investigated effect of a one-year treatment in type 1 patients.

Their randomized study tests adjunct metformin treatment in patients with persistent inadequate control. Readers get trial evidence on borrowing a type 2 drug for type 1 care. Even a modest insulin-sparing effect matters over a lifetime of injections.
plos-pone-0007463: Powdery mildew fungi infect nearly 10,000 kinds of plants, constantly outrunning plant defenses. This study found their weapons — virulence effector proteins — evolve in step with a family of jumping genes called LINE-1 retrotransposons. The coevolution suggests the jumping genes help the fungus reinvent its attack tools, explaining how the parasite adapts so fast.
plos-pone-0007563: Muscle stem cells face a choice: become muscle or become fat. This study shows an enzyme called RNase L helps decide, regulating the cells' potential to go either way. The finding adds a new control switch to the maintenance and repair of skeletal muscle.
plos-pone-0007663: Brain support cells called astrocytes make a protein, GFAP, whose variants may mark disease. This study used a purified antibody to reveal a specific astrocyte subtype — and found that unpurified serum falsely lights up nerve fibers in Alzheimer's samples. The caution matters for anyone reading GFAP stains in dementia research.
plos-pone-0007763: Small differences in mitochondrial DNA may shape personality. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Kishida and colleagues tested whether the A10398G variant in mitochondrial DNA relates to temperament in healthy young Japanese adults. Earlier work had linked mitochondrial variants to bipolar disorder, but healthy temperament was uncharted. The association analysis probes how our cells' power plants might nudge mood and behavior.
plos-pone-0007863: A newly found population of regulatory T cells lacks the classic Foxp3 marker yet still suppresses immunity. This mouse study showed their function depends on interferon-gamma, nitric oxide, and direct contact with targets. The alternative regulators expand the immune system's peacekeeping roster.
plos-pone-0007963: Thin metal films can act as 'superlenses' beating the diffraction limit. This study defined the operating regime for imaging fluorescent molecules with such lenses. The physics paves the way for seeing single molecules with unprecedented clarity.
plos-pone-0008063: The Notch signal shapes nearly every tissue, and this study found it regulated at the RNA level too. In fly embryos, Notch messenger RNA is controlled through its 3' processing. The early checkpoint adds a new layer to a famous pathway.
plos-pone-0008163: White sharks vanish offshore for months, and this study followed them. Tagging eastern Pacific sharks revealed their shared offshore foraging area and its environment. The first detailed portrait of the sharks' open-ocean life informs conservation of a mysterious migration.
plos-pone-0008263: Skin stem cells were coaxed toward becoming germ cells. This 2009 study differentiated primordial germ cell-like cells in vitro from skin-derived stem cells. The provocative result blurs the line between body and reproductive cells.
plos-pone-0008363: Smoking mothers' risks were found traveling in packs. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Lanting's team showed socioeconomic, behavioral, and newborn risks cluster in pregnant smokers. Quitting aids exist but national impact was unmeasured. The clustering means ills pile onto the same families. The pack pattern argues for bundled help.
plos-pone-0008463: A Parkinson's protein's toxic patch was pinned. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Jorgensen's team showed the WD40 domain is required for LRRK2's neuron-killing activity. Mutations in LRRK2 are the most common genetic cause of Parkinson's disease. The protein's enzymatic core is flanked by interaction domains. The WD40 requirement flags the patch as a drug target.
plos-pone-0008563: Nerve endings got a calcium ear. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Chen's team found the calcium-sensing receptor runs presynaptic outside calcium signals in rat cortex nerve ends. The receptor dials how much signal chemical pours out. The ear's role was unknown. The find adds a new knob to brain talk.
plos-pone-0008663: An immune-storm disease got a missing-brake clue. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Nold-Petry's team found interferon gamma fails to induce the calming IL-18 binding protein in familial hemophagocytosis. The runaway immune attack lacks its brake. The missing induction was mapped. The clue suggests treatment targets.
plos-pone-0008763: Lab-grown eye cells got a transplant recipe. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Lamba's team made photoreceptors from human induced pluripotent stem cells and transplanted them. The lab-grown light sensors were purified. The transplant method was validated. The recipe advances vision-restoration therapy.
plos-pone-0008863: A virus-tool enzyme's key bits got found. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Liu's team broke key bits of phage PhiC31's DNA-joining enzyme to find the must-haves. The bit-break map was run. The map aids gene-tool building.
plos-pone-0008963: Reef grazers' name tags got a coral check. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Burkepile and Hay found which grazers matter for seaweed shifts and coral growth. The grazer-by-grazer effects were logged. The check steers reef care.
plos-pone-0009063: Liver cells' fat genes got a TNF-alpha read. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Pandey's team showed TNF-alpha favors lipid and steroid metabolism genes in HepG2 cells. The expression-network analysis was run. The read informs liver-disease science.
plos-pone-0009163: Gene hush got a stall-spot map. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Tao's team mapped where gene hush stalls the copy machine. The stall-spot trick was logged. The map feeds gene science. The stall spots sit at developmental genes.
plos-pone-0009263: HIV drug resistance got a pooled deep-read. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Ji's team used pooled pyrosequencing for HIV drug-resistance surveillance. The high-throughput method was validated. The deep read speeds public-health monitoring.
plos-pone-0009363: Gene teamwork got a math test bed. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Edwards's team built a math test bed for gene teamwork. The test bed was checked. The bed feeds gene-hunt science. The bed handles gene pairs.
plos-pone-0011463: Around puberty, the brain rewires itself dramatically, and dopamine neurons are central to the remodel. This research paper finds that rodent dopamine neurons switch on UNC-5 — a receptor that steers growing nerve fibers — right at peri-puberty. The timing suggests adolescence opens a window when guidance cues redirect dopamine wiring, a clue to why the teenage brain is so changeable.
plos-pone-0011563: The butterfly Bicyclus anynana wears different coats across seasons, and a dark-larva mutation offered a genetic window. This research paper characterizes the mutation's genetic basis, body changes, and physiology. The three-angle portrait shows how a single mutation ripples from DNA to whole-animal form.
plos-pone-0011663: Card players study faces — and it shifts their bets. This research paper shows people's wagers change with the faces across the table. The finding proves social reads sneak into even cold math about risk, a very human leak in logic.
plos-pone-0011763: The protein HLA-G quiets immunity so mothers tolerate their babies — and tumors steal the trick. gerald-wales-historical-works-forester-1:
Gerald of Wales was a twelfth-century churchman who traveled Ireland and Wales and wrote about both with gusto. Thomas Forester translated his works for Bohn's series in 1863. This volume gathers the Topography of Ireland, the Conquest of Ireland, the Itinerary, and the Description of Wales.

Gerald reports strange beasts, wonders, and werewolves along with roads, rivers, and battles. He gossips, he moralizes, and he keeps a sharp eye on everything he passes. His Wales and Ireland are the wild Celtic fringe as a keen insider-outsider saw them. Few medieval travelers write with such life. Forester's one-volume gathering remains a handy door into Gerald's world.
liber-monstrorum-haupt-1863:
The Liber monstrorum, the Book of Monsters, is an early medieval Latin work by an unknown author. Moriz Haupt's critical edition of 1863 supplies this text. In three books it lists monstrous peoples, beasts, and serpents, the marvels that early medieval readers placed at the edges of the world.

Some entries echo reports from Pliny and the Alexander tales. Others sound like garbled travelers' news given a Latin polish. The author now and then doubts his own reports, which makes the book feel honest. Haupt's edition fixed the text for modern study. It remains the Dark Ages' own field guide to the uncanny.
neckam-de-naturis-rerum-1863:
Alexander Neckam, an English schoolman of the twelfth century, wrote De naturis rerum, on the natures of things. Thomas Wright edited it for the Rolls Series in 1863. Neckam taught at Oxford, and his book gathers the natural knowledge of his age with a teacher's care.

Beasts, birds, winds, and waters pass under his review, each with tales and morals attached. He reports marvels beside plain facts, as his century expected. His sharp mind sorts what he can and repeats what he cannot test. The work shows medieval England learning about its own world. Wright's edition made this schoolman's survey a standard source for students of medieval science.
